1:
Robertson and Calvin both mark this as a hinge. Robertson says Luke begins the second part of his book here, Antioch replacing Jerusalem as the centre and Paul replacing Peter, since Jerusalem had hesitated too long and the glory would now belong to Antioch. Calvin calls Paul's appointment a key by which the kingdom was opened to us: the covenant had been concluded properly with the Jews; Peter's errand to Cornelius was thought almost a prodigy and might have passed for a privilege granted to a few, but here God openly appoints apostles of the Gentiles. Whether the prophets and teachers are two ranks or one they cannot agree. Robertson makes the Greek particles divide the five three and two; Ellicott keeps the offices distinct, prophecy implying a direct message and teaching a systematic instruction; Barnes and Lightfoot merge them, Lightfoot because Antioch was not yet mature enough for teachers lacking prophecy; Henry has them prophets by occasional inspiration and teachers by settled office at once.

The names draw brief and conflicting notes. Ellicott takes Niger for a mark of African complexion, added to distinguish this Simeon from others and possibly from Simon of Cyrene; Robertson suggests he may be that very man who carried the cross. On Lucius both reject the identification with the author of the book: Ellicott because the names are radically distinct, Robertson because, though the name is a form of Luke, it is certainly not the physician. Manaen's upbringing with the tetrarch draws Robertson's remark that the gospel was reaching the higher classes, and Wesley's that he was freed from a court's temptations. Lightfoot adds a small point with a large consequence: Antioch already had prophets of its own when others came down from Jerusalem, so the sending out was done by that church's settled ministers, not by visitors.

The word for their ministering is disputed. Robertson traces it to the Attic orators who served the state at their own cost, and notes that our word liturgy grows from it; Ellicott finds behind it the ministry of priests and Levites. Calvin turns hard on that line, the word being also used of sacrifices and pressed into service for the mass; he answers that the verb is plural, so every one of them must have said mass, and that the only priesthood Christ left is that each man offer himself and ministers sacrifice souls with the gospel's spiritual sword. On the fast, Lightfoot and Clarke explain the Jewish practice of the second and fifth days, but Lightfoot refuses to build on it: bold to suppose the church kept weekly fasts, bolder that it kept the Jewish days, most audacious to imagine it fasted on the sabbath. Gill agrees it was no sabbath.

That the separating was not an ordination is nearly unanimous. Barnes says the word designates rather than ordains, and the office cannot be the apostolate, since Saul was called to that by revelation and Barnabas was no apostle; the appointment was to one enterprise, ended when they returned. Wesley is blunter, that Paul was ordained long before and not by man, and this was only inducting him to his province. Robertson calls it a solemn consecration to a missionary task, and adds that Antioch gave goodwill and no money, so the two financed the journey themselves, Philippi being the first church to pay, as Philippians 4:15 shows. Clarke makes the same distinction: the call was God's, the sanction the church's. Calvin observes that they prayed not for guidance in choosing, all doubt being removed, but that God would make the shoulders of his servants equal to the burden. Lightfoot notes that three men laying hands on two matches the synagogue rule of three ordainers while departing from it in the gesture, Jewish ordination using no hands. Cyril cites the verse to prove the Spirit a living person, separating, calling and sending with authority.
4:
The clause about being sent forth is read with care. Gill says it is put in lest anyone think they were sent by men, and Robertson notes that Luke names the Spirit rather than the church at Antioch as the source of their authority. Clarke divides the sending in three: without the Spirit's influence they were not qualified to go, without his authority they had no right to go, without his direction they could not know where. Ellicott suspects more than a summary, and thinks a fresh revelation followed the consecration and settled the route. Calvin observes that no church election is mentioned at all, the calling being wholly divine, the church only receiving what God's hand offered. Henry makes it the ground of their courage: if the Holy Ghost sends them he will go with them and give success, so they fear no colours and venture cheerfully on a stormy sea out of Antioch, which had been a quiet harbour.

Why Cyprus, and not somewhere else, divides them. Chrysostom offers reasons and then withdraws them: no ill design was being hatched there and the word had already been sown, Antioch had teachers enough and Phoenicia lay near Palestine while Cyprus did not; but one may not raise the question of why and wherefore when the Spirit directs the movements, since they were not only ordained by him but sent out by him. Henry and Robertson answer it the other way, both noting that Barnabas was a native of the island, Henry adding that he would wish his own country to have the firstfruits of his labour. Cyril tells the same story from the Antioch end: Barnabas sent to help the work, Paul fetched from Tarsus as his fellow-combatant, the disciples first called Christians by a name he thinks the Spirit bestowed, then the prophets and the command to separate the two.

The geography is filled in from the classical writers. Lightfoot identifies the port as Seleucia of Pieria, citing Strabo that it is the first Syrian city beyond Cilicia, with Ptolemy's coordinates and Pliny's measurement of Syria from it, and gauges the Jewish population of Cyprus from the scale of the revolt in Trajan's time. Ellicott adds that the port lay sixteen miles from Antioch and bore the name of Seleucus Nicator, that the island was largely Greek, and that Aphrodite was its goddess, Paphos being the centre of a worship notorious for the licentiousness of her temple women; the copper named from the island and the short crossing to Syria had drawn a considerable Jewish population. Both derive Salamis from Teucer son of Telamon, and Gill adds that Solon was born there and ordered his ashes scattered through the province. On the modern town they differ, Gill making it Famagusta and Clarke Salina.

That they went to the synagogues first is noticed by all and defended by two. Chrysostom asks whether we mark that they preached to the Jews first so as not to make them more contentious; Robertson calls it Paul's settled rule. Calvin faces the objection: sent specially to the Gentiles, they seem to begin amiss; but when God made them teachers of the Gentiles he did not depose them from the office they held, so nothing hindered their labouring among both. On John's office they disagree. Robertson gives the word its literal sense of under-rower and takes it for the synagogue attendant, allowing that he may have helped in the baptising. Ellicott says it implies personal service rather than the diaconate, guesses at baptising and preparing for the Supper, and calls Mark the courier of the apostolic church. Barnes and Clarke keep him to minor offices and travel arrangements, so the two might give themselves wholly to the doctrine; Calvin denies this outright, the word meaning not private or bodily service but help in preaching. Wesley says only that they used every opportunity offered.
6:
Gill, Clarke and Ellicott prefer the reading that has them cross the whole island, as the geography requires, Salamis lying east and Paphos west. Calvin refuses to read the silence about that journey as failure: Luke would never have passed over a general repulse, and it was enough to say they were not idle in teaching, since he is hurrying to a famous story. On the town itself they pile up antiquities. Gill derives the name from a Phoenician phrase for the corner of corners, both towns lying at the extremity, and refuses the fable of Pygmalion's ivory statue; Robertson places new Paphos eight miles north of the old, on a fine Roman road; Barnes gives the island's length as near a hundred and seventy miles. Clarke thinks no town in the world more dissolute, and notes that temple and city alike were thrown down by an earthquake, no vestige left. Calvin draws the conclusion the others leave implicit, that the goodness of God is the more wonderful for making the light of the gospel pierce so filthy a den.

The title given to Sergius Paulus is where the historical notes converge, because it was long held against Luke. Robertson states the charge plainly, that Cyprus was an imperial province under a propraetor and not a senatorial one under a proconsul, and answers that this held only until Augustus transferred it, adding that inscriptions dated within a year or two of this visit name proconsuls of Cyprus, one found at Soli carrying the name Paulus, in his judgment this very man. Ellicott tells the same history, noting that Strabo's description of Cyprus as a military province had led some to question the accuracy of the record, and that coins survive from the reign of Claudius naming a proconsul of the island. Clarke gives the rule in a sentence, imperial provinces receiving propraetors and senatorial ones proconsuls, and Barnes appeals to Lardner.

The man himself is read sympathetically. Barnes takes the epithet for intelligent and learned, perhaps for candid, a man of liberal views and inquiring mind, remarking how seldom men of rank will listen to the ministers of God. Wesley says he was not overswayed by Elymas but wished to inquire further; Clarke, that he did not persecute the preachers but sent for them to hear for himself, and speculates that his conversion is why his name was struck from the consular lists. Calvin reads his superstition as a symptom: wanting something better than his childhood religion, he had been drawn aside into various follies, and now sends for the apostles of his own accord, having conceived a fear of a God he did not yet know. Robertson finds it the more amazing that such a man was the sorcerer's victim, and recalls Juvenal's picture of the emperor on Capri surrounded by his Chaldaeans.

What Elymas means divides them. Barnes and Clarke insist it interprets the word for sorcerer and not the name Bar-jesus, Clarke complaining of the strange etymologies invented to support the other view and deriving it from the Arabic for knowledge. Gill takes that other view, that Elymas renders Bar-jesus, and canvasses several derivations. Lightfoot asks whether the second half of Bar-jesus is a proper name or a common noun, notes that the Syriac reads it as son of a swelling or a wound, and concludes that Elymas can be no interpretation of it if the name is proper. On the opposition they agree. Barnes and Ellicott trace it to self-interest, the impostor seeing his standing would end if the proconsul were won, and Barnes generalises that love of popularity and power is often why men oppose the gospel; Robertson says he persisted, unwilling to lose his prize. Calvin turns it on the reader: the same contest goes on with babblers who sell their smoke, and where no magician is at hand Satan supplies enticements enough.
9:
The change of name is the first question, and the sharpest. Ellicott finds it impossible not to connect the new name with the conversion just made, and gives three advantages: it was close enough in sound to fall within the practice that turned Silas into Silvanus, it was Roman rather than Greek and so suited a witness to be borne one day in the imperial city, and it linked him to the illustrious convert. Robertson rejects that outright: the word also does not mean the name was new, since as a Jew and Roman citizen he had carried both all along, and he dismisses the borrowing theory as carrying an element of vulgarity impossible in such a man. Lightfoot and Gill explain the double name by the Jewish custom of one name at home and another abroad, Lightfoot adding that Luke gives the Gentile name alone now that he is declared apostle of the Gentiles. Barnes reports the Latin sense of little or dwarfish, guessed to fit his size; Clarke prefers a Hebrew root meaning wonderful, citing Jerome.

The denunciation that follows is defended before it is explained. Calvin argues that Paul had no hope of doing good by mild dealing; we must begin with doctrine and admonish those not yet plainly obstinate, and Paul attacks the man only when he sees him maliciously fighting the doctrine of godliness; so must we deal with desperate enemies, above all when they stop the way before others. Lest the anger seem excessive, he points out that Luke names the Spirit's inspiration as Paul's guide, so the heat of zeal is not to be blamed. The words are weighed closely. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott trace the second noun from a root meaning ease in working through shiftiness to trickery, Clarke saying it defines a juggler exactly; Robertson says Paul pictured a slick rascal with deadly accuracy; Wesley divides the charges, guile for the false prophet, mischief for the magician. Both hear the title son of the devil set against the name son of Jesus that he bore.

On the blindness they agree, and the agreement is about mercy. Clarke says every word proves Paul's immediate inspiration, since by the Spirit he discerned the man's state and foretold a blindness of which there was yet no sign; but in judgment God remembers mercy, the blindness being temporary and meant to soften, and he reports the old tradition that Elymas was afterwards converted. Ellicott suggests the penalty may have been the apostle's own choice in prayer, remembering how his own blindness had led him to the light, and finds a moral fitness in blinding a man whose sin was fighting against light; being for a season, it was meant to heal. Robertson calls it blindness for blindness, darkness without for darkness within. Calvin alone treats the power as a problem: the apostles had a whip as well as a healing hand, as Peter showed on Ananias, but since miracles should resemble a gentle and merciful Christ, examples of the contrary power were rare, and never at their own discretion.

The conversion at the end is read carefully. Robertson notes the objection that a Roman proconsul could not be converted by a miracle, and answers that the teaching about the Lord astonished him as much as the sign; no baptism is recorded, and he need not have lost his office. Calvin puts the sequence carefully: reverence for doctrine is faith's beginning, so the miracle showed him Paul was sent of God and he began to reverence what he had doubted; and if God now upholds faith without such signs, we must not murmur as though our condition were worse. Clarke calls the word a two-edged sword, striking the sinner with judgment, the honest inquirer with conviction. Cyril, expounding the power at work in the apostles, insists the Spirit is one and undivided though his operations vary.
13:
A change of order is noticed by three. Clarke observes that Luke names Barnabas first up to this point and afterwards always Paul; Ellicott says the phrase, literally those about Paul, marks his new position as leader; Robertson calls it a neat Greek idiom for a man and his followers, and quotes the judgment that the greatness of Barnabas is nowhere clearer than in recognising Paul's superiority and accepting second place. Why John Mark turned back nobody knows, and each guesses differently. Barnes suspects fear of danger or alarm at unknown country, Wesley the fatigue or the risk; Clarke thinks he went to see his mother and Peter at Jerusalem, and Ellicott allows either hardship or the mother, the famine there being an excuse a son might plead. Robertson suggests something sharper, that the cousin of Barnabas may not have relished the change of leadership. Calvin calls it softness plainly, says Luke records it because it later caused a sorry quarrel, and that in noting one man's weakness he praises the others' constancy.

Perga is described, then explained away. Barnes makes it the metropolis of Pamphylia, on the Cestrus some way from the sea, with a famous temple of Diana near; Clarke, since it is no seaport, supposes they sailed up the river, reckoning it a great way inland, while Ellicott puts the city seven miles from the mouth. That nothing is told of preaching there Ellicott explains by the absence of synagogues, the apostles having made the synagogue their base. Henry accepts the silence as ordinary selection, since the history of the apostles' travels, like Christ's, passes by much worth recording, for if all were written the world could not contain the books. Gill fills the gap from the other end, tracing a church at Perga through its martyrs under Decius, its bishops in three later centuries, and its rank as metropolitan.

Why they left so soon Robertson admits is unclear, and reports two conjectures, malaria driving them to the hills after Mark's desertion, or summer heat having driven the population there already; he adds that the climb over the rough mountain road was perilous enough to stand among the dangers of 2 Corinthians 11:26, and that the illness behind his first Galatian preaching may belong here. On the city they reached, the geographers correct the label. Barnes says flatly that Antioch was not in Pisidia but in Phrygia, and was called Pisidian only to distinguish it from the Syrian one; Robertson agrees, adding that it was a Roman colony and free city, like Philippi. Lightfoot notes that Strabo's list of thirteen Pisidian cities omits it, though Pliny and Ptolemy place it there. Ellicott supplies its founding by Seleucus Nicator, its position on the Taurus slopes the travellers had to cross, and the Roman citizenship it held from Augustus. Clarke notes only that twelve towns bore the name.

The sitting down is read as a claim. Lightfoot says the word is the ordinary one for anybody who teaches, so even if the rulers knew nothing else of them they could gather that these were preachers. Ellicott agrees the act showed them teachers and not hearers, taking the rabbi's seat, and amounted to asking leave to speak; he adds that the synagogue excluded the priestly element altogether, lay preaching by trained men being established practice. Robertson agrees. Barnes and Clarke remark that though the mission was to the Gentiles they offered the gospel to the Jews first at every opportunity; Wesley notes only that this Antioch is not the one they came from. Calvin uses the sabbath assembly to make a point about holy days: the institution figured a spiritual rest now fulfilled in Christ, so the figure is past, but God had regard also to the practical use, that men free from business might keep their assemblies, and we should keep our own days to that end.
15:
The lectionary is described almost identically by four. Gill counts the sections of the law at fifty-three, read through in a year and finished at the close of tabernacles on the day called the rejoicing of the law, and notes a rarer usage spreading them over three years; Ellicott gives fifty-three or fifty-four and dates the practice soon after the return from Babylon; Clarke refers to his own table of the lessons, made with indescribable labour; Robertson adds that Antiochus banned the law, the prophets being read instead until the Maccabees restored both. Ellicott then does what none of the others attempt and fixes the very sabbath: Paul's opening words echo Deuteronomy 1:31, the lesson appointed for the forty-fourth sabbath of the year, and the prophetic lesson set beside it is the chapter of Isaiah he also quotes, so that he began from what the congregation had that moment heard.

In what language it was heard divides them. Lightfoot raises the question directly, granting that Hellenist synagogues are supposed to have read the Greek Bible but doubting whether Greek was understood in Pisidia, since Strabo lists the Pisidian tongue as one of four there and distinguishes it from Greek. Clarke presses the same difficulty from the same passage. Ellicott has no doubt, holding it almost certain that Paul used Greek throughout the journey and, from the echoes of the lesson, absolutely certain here. On the invitation Barnes and Robertson agree that the rulers chose readers and speakers alike, Barnes adding that they could punish and excommunicate, and that these two were asked as visiting Jews. Wesley thinks it a decency the apostles would hardly have omitted, to ask leave by a message sent in before the service.

Calvin makes the order of that service a lesson. No prayers are mentioned, he notes, though certainly they were not omitted, Luke reckoning only what belonged to teaching; and he calls it a notable place, the law and prophets holding the first room, nothing being set before the Church that is not drawn from that fountain, while those able to teach came second as interpreters of what was read. He gathers besides that Scripture was kept back from none, all alike being admitted to the reading. On Paul's rising there is a small conflict: Robertson says the Jewish custom was to sit and the Greek to stand, leaving open which he followed, while Chrysostom calls standing the custom of the Jews, and Gill takes the rising for a sign that he accepted the invitation. Ellicott says the gesture was a wave of the hand for silence rather than a beckoning, a graphic touch he thinks came from someone present.

The strategy of the opening is admired by all who mention it. Barnes observes that to begin at once with the Messiah would have raised their prejudice and rage, so Paul first shows himself a firm believer in the Scriptures and no despiser of their fathers' doctrine. Clarke says he proves his case not by the rhetorician's arts but by plain history. Calvin puts the argument at its root: Paul must show Israel excelling the nations in this one thing, that the Saviour was promised them, so all their privileges hung on that promise and moved toward it. Chrysostom watches the courtesy of it, that Paul praises them before he argues, and does not say ye proselytes, a term of disadvantage, but ye that fear God. Who those were the others explain: Clarke makes them converts to the Jewish religion, Wesley allows proselytes or heathens either, Robertson sees a crowd of Gentiles like Cornelius, and in them the opening Paul needed to the pagan world. Chrysostom adds the note about Barnabas, who gave place to the man he had fetched from Tarsus, as John everywhere gave way to Peter, though Barnabas was the more looked up to, both eyeing only the common advantage.
17:
Ellicott notes that Paul follows Stephen's plan, opening with a recapitulation Israelites never tired of hearing; Wesley says these six verses contain the whole sum of the Old Testament, conciliating the hearers while convincing them of their duty. Calvin adds that the preface proved Paul brought in nothing new to draw them from Moses, calling the one God of all nations the God of this people, to whom he had bound himself. Then a textual question changes the sentence's tone. The word rendered suffered their manners differs by one letter from a word meaning to nurse, or carry as a father carries his child. Ellicott prefers the second, the better manuscripts supporting it and the sense fitting the conciliatory drift far better than a word implying reproach; Robertson agrees, though the critics print the other. Clarke calls the two of equal value; Barnes and Calvin keep the harsher reading, Calvin finding in it the mercy of God bearing with a people he knew to be stubborn. Lightfoot argues from the qualifying about that the forty years may mean the span between the decree of exclusion and the entry into Canaan.

The seven nations are listed by Gill, Barnes and Clarke, and Lightfoot notes with Clarke that the rabbis use the phrase as a fixed term. On the dividing of the land Ellicott and Robertson agree the better text reads gave for an inheritance rather than divided by lot, the two verbs having been confused in the Greek Old Testament too. Then comes the hardest verse in the speech. Clarke reports that Scaliger called it the cross of chronologers, and Barnes that it has exercised all their ingenuity, since four hundred and fifty years for the judges will not fit inside the four hundred and eighty Kings allows between the exodus and the temple. Ellicott cuts the knot from the manuscripts, the better reading attaching the number not to the judges but to what precedes, so the years cover the interval from the choosing of the fathers and the judges follow after; Robertson reads it the same way.

Saul is handled briefly and with some tenderness. Ellicott thinks it natural the apostle should dwell on the hero-king of his own tribe, having just laid the name aside; Robertson notes that Paul names Benjamin with pride and says nothing of Saul's sin. Barnes and Clarke both complain that the translators dropped the familiar spelling of his father's name. The forty years are a difficulty, no such figure appearing in the Old Testament. Robertson and Ellicott find it in Josephus, Ellicott supporting it from the age of Ish-bosheth at his father's death against Saul's youth when anointed; Barnes cites it but records that its division of the reign has been shown impossible; Clarke reckons from the anointing to the death, Wesley by including the years of Samuel's judging.

The commendation of David is where they divide most sharply. Clarke, following Benson, restricts it to the public character: David ruled according to the divine will, allowed no idolatry and claimed no absolute power. Wesley presses harder: David was such at that time and not at all times, and in the matter of Uriah was as far from being a man after God's own heart as Saul himself, so that to take the phrase for his whole character is a gross and dangerous mistake. Calvin turns the other way: the title is cited less to praise the man than to make the Jews attentive to Christ, since by extolling David so highly the speaker lifts their minds to the one David figured; and the added son of Jesse enlarges the grace, Jesse having been a keeper of cattle. Ellicott and Robertson agree the saying is a composite quotation in the rabbinic manner, joining Psalm 89:20 to the word spoken to Samuel, Robertson noting the argument that so free a quotation tells for the report's genuineness.
23:
Calvin makes the promise itself the argument: in sending Christ the Lord had regard only to his own faithfulness, so the gospel gains credit from the fact that Christ came not suddenly and unspoken of, but was given in his time as one promised from the beginning; the promises were so familiar that the Jews called him by no other name than Son of David. Ellicott adds a shrewd guess, that the names of Jesus and John can hardly have been unknown even in remote Pisidia, since no Jew could have kept a feast at Jerusalem for years past without hearing of one or the other; Paul's tone is that of a man assuming vague knowledge and offering to clear it. Wesley says the same of the Baptist, whose preaching raised so loud an alarm it must have been heard of as far as Pisidia.

Why John is cited Calvin explains: Paul proves he preaches no false Christ but the one that forerunner commended, and though a man's word could not settle so weighty a matter, almost everybody took John for a prophet, so the authority is a crier sent from heaven and not a private person. He adds that John's question is not a doubter's but a rebuke, the Jews having falsely given him the honour of the Messiah, and that a witness who refuses honour offered him deserves more credit. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all note that the words quoted are not the precise words of any Gospel though the sense is the same, Robertson adding that the Greek asks what rather than who, a question of character and not identity.

The renewed address is read as deliberate: Gill thinks the title men one the Jews claimed for themselves and denied the nations, while Clarke objects that the phrase should have been rendered brethren simply. Ellicott observes that the two classes are again pointedly set side by side, the stock of Abraham and those who fear God. Over the word that follows they differ quietly: Robertson takes the salvation as sent to both classes together and calls the tense a climax, the glorious promise arriving in one day; Barnes keeps it narrower, sent particularly to the Jewish people. Calvin sees a pastoral purpose in the courtesy, Paul speaking them fair so it may not grieve them to leave the scribes and priests they revered; and though the gate stood open to the Gentiles, the Jews were not thrown down from their standing. Cyril, marvelling at the same preacher, calls it a wise dispensation that the former persecutor was given more to write than the rest, that the doctrine might stand beyond question.

The handling of Jerusalem is admired for its restraint. Barnes says the verse is meant not to reproach but to introduce the death, Paul speaking of the murderers with tenderness and softening the crime as far as it can be softened; Clarke calls it a gentle excuse for the persecuting priests. Both then turn the excuse into an indictment: they did not know him because they did not know the prophets, and did not know the prophets, read every sabbath though these were, because they had no desire to know God's will. Robertson holds the same balance: the ignorance lessened their guilt without removing it, being willing ignorance and prejudice. Wesley finds the proof in the sentence they passed, condemning an innocent man showing they had not understood the prophecies about him. Ellicott presses the irony further, that Paul appeals to the very synagogue ritual his sermon began from, which witnesses not to a conquering Messiah but to the chief of sufferers. Calvin explains why the point had to be made: Jerusalem was God's sanctuary and the light of the world, so receiving one cast out of the temple looked like leaving the Church, and that objection alone was strong enough to overthrow the whole sermon.
28:
Calvin explains why the innocence had to be stated: we could not be justified by a death suffered for the man's own crimes, so he must be guiltless if his death was to satisfy for the world's sins. Gill notes that the suborned witnesses could not support their charges and that Pilate declared the innocence repeatedly; Barnes and Ellicott set out the manoeuvre, the council condemning him for blasphemy without proof and then shifting the charge before the governor. Robertson observes that Paul knew the innocence though no Gospel was yet written. On the burial three feel a difficulty, since the men who took the body down were not those who killed him. Barnes answers that Paul does not say the same persons did both, only that Jews did all of it; Robertson that the details are not distinguished; Calvin admits it seems contrary to the gospel history. Ellicott finds more in the clause about fulfilling what was written, Paul having learned the evangelists' own prophetic reading; and Calvin adds that the stumbling-block of the cross falls away once it is seen that the Son of God obeyed his Father's decree. Wesley sums up: so far they could go, no farther.

Clarke and Calvin make the resurrection carry the weight. Clarke argues that God alone raises the dead and would not do it except on an extraordinary occasion, so the rising itself proves the innocence just asserted; Calvin says Paul dwells longer here because none could be persuaded to seek salvation in a death unless almighty power had appeared in the raising. The witnesses are pressed as evidence. Ellicott hears a man who had talked with them and satisfied himself of their testimony, and insists the tense means they are his witnesses still; Robertson calls them men not easily deceived; Clarke urges that the thing was lately done and many were still alive.

At the announcement of good tidings Calvin sees Paul claiming an apostle's honour, bringing in nothing new but the fulfilling of a doctrine his hearers already confessed; Robertson calls this the heart of the message. Then the text becomes uncertain. Ellicott says the better manuscripts read almost without exception unto our children, the received reading looking like a correction toward an easier sense. Robertson reports the variants as worse and follows the editors who treat them all as a primitive corruption of a simple to us; he adds that the raising up here is not the resurrection but the sending, two different raisings standing in the passage. Calvin uses the word children against allegory: Paul means natural descendants, and men who dissolve all into figures empty the covenant made with Abraham's seed.

The reference to the second psalm carries its own variant. Clarke reports that one great manuscript and several fathers read the first psalm, that Griesbach admitted it, and that he thinks the evidence insufficient; he explains the difficulty from Hebrew manuscripts in which the first two psalms are written as one. Ellicott and Robertson give the same account, the present first psalm having sometimes been treated as a prelude with the numbering begun at the second. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic side from a discussion of how many psalms the daily prayers answer to, turning on whether the psalm beginning why do the heathen rage counts among them. On the quoted words they divide. Barnes takes them as calling Jesus Son of God because God raised him; Wesley answers that he was Son from eternity, so the sense is that God this day declared him such, the begetting dated with peculiar beauty from the day he seemed born out of the earth anew. Henry makes the rising the great proof of sonship, one who had life in himself being unable to be held by death. Cyril turns the verse against those who own one God but refuse the Father of Jesus Christ, contradicting their own prophets.
34:
Gill marks the turn, that the raising up of the last verse and the raising from the dead in this one are distinct articles. On the word corruption Barnes and Clarke agree that it cannot mean putrefaction, since the body in question never underwent it, but stands for death or the grave as its place and cause, so the clause means only that he should not die again. Robertson puts it by contrast, that he was not about to return as Lazarus did, and so is the firstfruits. Calvin draws out what hangs on it: the hope conceived from the resurrection would be slender and cold if he were still subject to change, and since he rose rather for our sake than his own, the perpetual life the Father gave him reaches to us.

The promise quoted next is not obviously about a resurrection, and they explain the connection differently. Lightfoot observes that everyone notices the phrase comes from the Greek of Isaiah, but few that by David the Messiah was there understood, which the rabbis Kimchi and Ibn Ezra had themselves remarked and the following verse confirms; so the sure mercies of David are the sure mercies of Christ. Clarke reaches the same conclusion, holding it evident from the application that the speaker took David to signify the Messiah. Ellicott concedes more: the words do not in themselves look like a Messianic prediction, but to minds saturated with the prophets they would be full of meaning, the sure mercies being the everlasting covenant to be fulfilled in one given as a leader and commander to the people. Wesley reads them as blessings promised to David in Christ, sure and solid to every believer, so that the resurrection necessarily follows, since without it they could not be given at all.

The second quotation is handled quickly. Gill notes that the versions vary between another psalm, another place and simply elsewhere. Robertson says the words prove that his body saw no corruption, a flat contradiction of those who deny a bodily resurrection. Calvin refers the reader back to the same text in Peter's first sermon rather than expound it twice, pausing only over the two Hebrew words behind the Greek, one taken from the grave as an insatiable gulf. Cyril, coming at the psalm under a different number, applies its earlier verses to those who refused Christ and chose Caesar for their king before reaching the clause about corruption.

The proof turns on the plain fact that David died. Clarke states it bluntly: David died, was buried and never rose, so the words can be applied to Jesus only. Barnes says the verse is designed to show the psalm could not refer to David and must relate to another. Calvin adds a qualification the others do not: the prophecy was fulfilled whole in Christ as head, yet takes place in all the members too, according to the measure of each. Over the clause about serving his own generation there is difficulty. Barnes calls it an unusual and almost unintelligible expression and canvasses the ancient versions; Robertson lays out three constructions and says each is grammatical and makes good sense; Ellicott takes it as ministering to his own generation and hears a contrast between the narrow limits of any man's service and the endless ministry of the Son of Man, adding that David slept by God's counsel when his work was done. Gill fills in what the service was, governing by wholesome laws, protecting property and promoting the worship of God. Wesley makes the same contrast and turns it on the reader, asking why anyone still in the world is here at all if not to serve the will of God, and whether he is serving it now; he adds that being gathered to the fathers concerns the soul and not the body only, and so supposes its immortality.
38:
Clarke sets out the conclusion as a chain: since God promised an endless succession to David's seed and David's family failed in the political kingdom, a spiritual kingdom must be meant; since the person promised was to see no corruption and David saw it; since Jesus wrought the works and suffered the indignities foretold, the inference is forced. Calvin marks the change of subject, from how salvation was purchased to Christ's office and power, the principal point being to know what good things we have by his coming; the opening words mean that nothing but sloth could keep them from a matter so plain. Ellicott notes that the Greek tense makes the forgiveness something proclaimed at that very moment, and that it is the keynote of this preaching as it had been of Peter's, the Baptist's and the Lord's own.

The next sentence draws the most comment. Robertson calls it a characteristic Greek period with the principal clause held to the end, the climax falling last and giving the heart of Paul's teaching. Ellicott renders the preposition strictly as in him, the sphere in which forgiveness is found rather than the instrument; and he finds it striking that in this earliest specimen of Paul's teaching the very word afterwards identified with him appears, in its forensic sense of acquitted. Calvin is blunter: Paul's meaning is plainly justification by faith alone, which his opponents resist as bitterly as obstinately. Gill lists what the righteousness is not, neither works of law nor evangelical obedience nor inward holiness nor even the grace of faith, but faith's object; and the acquittal is complete, from sins original and actual. Henry makes it exclusive, that believers and none else are justified, and states the reason simply: if anything is left charged upon the sinner he is undone. Wesley fixes the moment, the believer having actual forgiveness of all his sins at the very time of believing.

Wesley then makes an observation none of the others do. The law could not justify, and not merely cannot now but never could, having no expiation for presumptuous sins; and the division of the law into moral and ceremonial, so common among us, was not common among the Jews and is not in view here at all, Moses and Christ being simply set against each other. Barnes takes the milder line that the sacrifices were typical of a greater one they could not themselves supply. The warning that follows is read as deliberate. Calvin says the speaker had stiff-necked men before him, or some at least, and adds a chiding to his doctrine as though to soften stubbornness with a hammer; had they been willing he would have allured them sweetly, and even now he leaves room for repentance. Robertson guesses Paul had seen anger on some rabbinic faces; Barnes thinks the caution the more needed because the Jews held themselves safe; Wesley calls it weighty and seasonable, with no reproof yet added.

The closing quotation diverges from the Hebrew, and they all notice it. Barnes says it comes substantially from the Greek of Habakkuk 1:5, where the threat was of the Chaldean invasion; Clarke prints Hebrew, Greek and citation together; Ellicott notes that ye despisers stands where the Hebrew has ye among the heathen, and wonder and perish replaces wonder marvellously. Robertson observes that both despisers and perish are additions of the Greek version, and that Paul hurled a thunderbolt at the close. Calvin explains why the looser wording serves: by saying despisers rather than nations the speaker tells the Jews that the vengeance once brought on their fathers belongs to every despiser, so the threat reaches all ages. Ellicott adds that the prophet quoted supplied the axiom of Paul's life, that the just shall live by faith. Clarke says that never was a prophecy more pointedly applied, since these Jews persevered and their city and temple fell.
42:
Chrysostom explains the effect by the method. Paul not only won admiration at the time but planted a longing for a second hearing, dropping seeds as it were and declining to solve the questions he had raised or follow the subject to its end, his plan being to engage their goodwill rather than make them listless by casting all at once into their minds; he told them the fact that remission is announced through this man, but not the how. He notices too that from this point Paul is named first. Why some walked out is variously judged. Henry says they were so incensed at preaching addressed to themselves and not to the Gentiles that they would not bear it, and went out while Paul still spoke, in contempt of him and to the disturbance of the assembly, probably by agreement. Clarke identifies them as the despisers of the prophecy; Wesley supposes many went out before the sermon was done.

The next clause is one of the most unsettled in the chapter, and the disagreement is complete. Lightfoot puts the question fairly: the words will bear either they besought the Gentiles or the Gentiles besought them; the second has generally prevailed, but he asks what absurdity there would be in the first, and thinks the order of the Greek favours it, especially if the Jews had gone out offended and the apostles turned to those who stayed. Clarke reaches the same preference, the words bearing either but the former being more natural, the apostle asking the better-minded Gentiles to come again. Ellicott and Robertson cut the knot the other way, the better manuscripts having neither, since the word Gentiles is an explanatory addition; Robertson adds that the received text wrongly suggests the Jews were against Paul from the first, whereas both parties asked for the sermon again. Barnes reports the versions at length and concludes it is perhaps impossible to determine the true reading. Gill notes that several copies omit the clause about the synagogue; Calvin reads the phrase with the Jews, so the two went out while the assembly still sat.

On the day appointed they differ further. Ellicott insists the words mean the following sabbath and not, as the margin has it, the intervening week, though the other rendering is literally possible; Robertson takes the same sense from a late use of the adverb. Wesley reads it otherwise, as the sabbath the Jews still call the one falling between the first of Tisri and the day of expiation on the tenth. Clarke and Robertson both ask what kind of proselytes are meant, since the word commonly denotes those who had accepted circumcision while the rabbis used it also of proselytes of the gate, which both think likelier here. Ellicott observes that both classes followed and not one only, and guesses that in the intervening week the two supported themselves at their trade, tent-cloth being made everywhere in the towns under the Taurus.

The last clause leaves one more ambiguity, which Calvin alone states. The exhortation to continue in the grace of God may run either way. It may be that the Jews and proselytes urged Paul and Barnabas not to faint but stand stoutly, having occasion enough with combats prepared and constancy needed against the opposing faction; or that Paul and Barnabas received those who came courteously and strengthened them to persist in the grace they had received. Calvin allows both, preferring neither; the rest assume the second. Clarke glosses continuing as crediting the gospel, receiving its spirit and bringing forth its fruits, and so remaining under God's favour; Wesley adds the reason, that trials were at hand; Ellicott notes that the tense implies the persuading went on through the week. Gill pauses over the breaking up of the assembly, whether dismissed in order by the interpreter or broken up in the disorder the preaching had caused.
44:
The size of the gathering raises a practical problem. Ellicott points out that no synagogue could have held such a crowd, and offers two arrangements: the people thronged doors and windows while the apostles spoke within, or filled an open space and were addressed from the entrance. Robertson guesses that Paul spoke inside and Barnabas to the overflow. Clarke makes the point that people are not converted by public discourses only but by the private teaching and godly conduct of those who have received the truth, scattered through society as leaven in every place. Calvin takes the crowd as proof that the two had not idled between the sabbaths, though he suspects the hearers came in a quandary, hoping the matter would be settled by debate.

The envy is analysed with care. Barnes notes the word is properly zeal, and means indignation that such multitudes should want a message they themselves rejected. Ellicott draws it sharply: they heard the apostles addressing the crowd not in the condescending tone of men who could just tolerate a wealthy proselyte able to buy their favour, but as finding in every hearer a brother on the same level, redeemed by the same Christ; and this practical repudiation of their exclusive privileges was more than they could bear. Robertson insists these are not the proselytes of the previous verse but Jews who had cooled during the week under rabbinic influence; nothing is said of the rabbis, but he has no doubt they were the ringleaders, adding drily that no such crowds came when they were the speakers. Calvin makes it a rule that the rage of the wicked is inflamed whenever the light comes nearer.

The answer is read as a deliberate escalation. Calvin says the two were so far from discouraged that they inveighed more freely, having spared their hearers a little before; now that Christ is obstinately rejected they excommunicate them in their turn, from which he draws the rule that extreme severity is for the hopeless only. Wesley says flatly that hinderers must be publicly reproved. Ellicott sees the apostles following what they took for the divine plan, the Jews having been offered the privilege of being the channel of blessing to all families of the earth and, on refusing, losing the office; Robertson notes that Paul always keeps this order, the Jew first in privilege and penalty. Wesley catches the irony of the phrase about worthiness: they judged none but themselves worthy of eternal life, yet their rejection said as plainly as words that they were unworthy; and the turn to the Gentiles did not mean they left off preaching to Jews elsewhere, only that they would lose no more time here.

The closing citation draws the best remarks. Barnes observes that Paul appeals to the Old Testament rather than to the command of Jesus because his hearers acknowledged their own Scriptures but would have scorned a word of Jesus of Nazareth. Clarke generalises: the apostles could quote a pertinent scripture for everything they did, and in the things of God no minister should go farther than he can say it is written, taking care that quotations are fairly made and no detached clause produced because it happens to suit the system he wishes to establish. Ellicott calls it the first example of the train of thought by which this reader found in the prophets, where others found only Israel's exaltation, a purpose of love toward the whole heathen world, the germ of the argument later developed in Romans. On whom the words address they differ: Calvin says God speaks in Isaiah 49:6 to his Son and not to the apostles, allowing that much which Scripture gives Christ belongs to his ministers too, though not all, since to adorn them with titles proper to his person would be sacrilege; Gill refers the command instead to the enlarged commission after the resurrection.
48:
One clause divides them more sharply than anything else in the chapter. Clarke opens by saying the text has been most pitifully misunderstood, and insists on examining the word before fixing its meaning: the participle is neither the compound that would say fore-ordained nor the one that would say predestinated, but a simple form carrying no idea of pre-ordination. Wesley presses the same point from the time rather than the grammar: Luke speaks not of anything done from eternity but of what was done then through the preaching, so the ordination described is the one made at the very hour of hearing, those believing to whom God then gave power to believe. Ellicott suggests the rendering as many as were disposed for eternal life, and suspects that the English word ordained was itself chosen under the influence of the theology current when the version was made. Barnes reports the ancient versions, which render it destined or foreordained. Calvin takes the joy rather than the participle for his subject: the Gentiles rejoiced to learn they were not called suddenly, as though nothing had been decreed beforehand, but that what was foretold many years earlier was now fulfilled.

The spread that follows implies time. Ellicott says the phrase involves a long period of work, and not in the city only but in the border country where three provinces met, so every town and village showed a few men and women who no longer sacrificed to their country's gods nor were content with the synagogue, but met in small companies as disciples of a new Master. Calvin sees the parable of the leaven proved true, and Gill traces the church that grew there. The counter-attack is a study in influence. Ellicott recalls that their opponents compassed sea and land for one proselyte and found women the easier converts, and grants that such conversions had a good side as well as a bad. Robertson notes that with one synagogue only the Jews cannot have been numerous, though they had access to people of standing; Clarke and Gill agree the women were heathen matrons turned proselyte, wealthy enough to work on magistrates who were probably their own husbands.

Shaking the dust off is explained as a known sign. Calvin argues that Christ would not have prescribed an unknown gesture, so it was already a token of cursing among the Jews, meaning that God so detests the wicked that we must beware of fellowship lest we take their uncleanness. Clarke spells out its message, that you are worse than the heathen and your land accursed, so we dare not let its dust cleave to our feet; and Jews returning from heathen countries shook their feet at the border. Ellicott points out that the act is literal obedience to a command of Christ, fair evidence that it had reached these two as well as the Twelve, and that its symbolism reverses the usual reckoning: the unbelieving Jews, not the heathen, make dust unclean.

The chapter ends on joy. Barnes observes that it came in the midst of persecution, evidence that the gospel can fill the soul in the severest trials. Robertson adds that the blood of the martyrs is still the seed of the church. Clarke writes the finest sentences: in the world they had tribulation, in Christ peace, and in their Master's work they always had their Master's wages; a Christian's happiness lies beyond the reach of earthly disturbance, so the martyrs were happier in the flames than their persecutors on beds of down. Calvin weighs two constructions and prefers to say they were filled with joy because the Spirit's grace reigned in them. Gill asks whether the disciples meant are the apostles, glad to be counted worthy to suffer, or the converts; and Cyril, on the same gladness, sets beside it the charge to rejoice in the Lord always, since redemption has drawn near.
